subject: Post-call recap: AeroWorks burst & streaming SLOs + next steps
messages:
From: Olga Petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.com>
To: devops@aeroworks.com (Samir Patel)
Cc: rishi.malhotra@redwood.com, marissa.cole@redwood.com
Date: Mon, 30 Jul 2028 16:12:00 +0000
Subject: Post-call recap: AeroWorks burst & streaming SLOs + next steps

Hi Samir —

Thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap + our proposed next steps so we have a single place to iterate. Overall we heard: a low-latency streaming assistant is the primary use case (human-facing), with occasional synchronous batch jobs for nightly enrichment. Key targets you mentioned:

- Business SLOs we should validate: 95th percentile end-to-end token latency target <= 200 ms for streaming flows; first-token latency target <= 150 ms where possible.
- Concurrency & throughput: steady concurrent streams ~400 - 600; short-duration bursts up to ~1,500 concurrent requests (peaks lasting 3-8 minutes).
- Streaming characteristics: average reply length ~60 tokens, typical session ~3-4 turns, many short sessions (high fan-out).
- Availability / fallback: ability to maintain service during regional disruption and automatic fallback to a functional model variant.

From Redwood's side we propose the following starting plan to hit those SLOs:

- Warm pool: prewarmed instances target = 30 (initial) with a recommendation to test up to 40 for worst-case 95th token latency.
- Scale-up time objective: cold->ready within 90s for vertical scale; autoscale can be tuned to 45-60s for aggressive burst pools.
- Queueing behavior: soft queue capacity 5,000 requests with per-request soft timeout 30s (configurable) and prioritized draining for interactive traffic.
- Model variant: q4_0 quantized variant for production PoC to reduce token-level latency.
- Observability signals: p50/p95/p99 token latency, cold_start_rate, queue_latency_ms, prewarm_utilization, and stream-first-token latency.

Attached: AeroWorks-performance-requirements.xlsx (workload summary) and a short priming plan we suggest.

As next steps can you: 1) confirm the 95p target (<=200ms) and first-token target (<=150ms) for streaming, 2) share a 48-72h representative traffic trace (or the traffic profile file), and 3) confirm willingness to run a 2-week PoC with synthetic priming during business hours + real-traffic shadowing?

I'll loop in Marissa for the solutions engineering kick-off and Rishi for the PoC engineering plan. If these targets look off, flag them and we'll reframe.

Thanks —
Olga
Director, Strategic Solutions
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: AeroWorks burst & streaming SLOs + next steps

Olga —

Thanks for the concise summary. Couple clarifications from our side so you can size the PoC correctly:

1) Streaming breakdown: we will stream tokens incrementally; average turn is ~60 tokens but we do see longer reply cases up to 350 tokens (rare).
2) Traffic peaks: our internal telemetry shows peak simultaneous sessions historically hitting ~480 RPS, but marketing launches can spike to 1,200-1,600 concurrent sessions for 4-6 minutes.
3) First-token SLAs are critical for UX. We want to target <=150ms for first token in the PoC and are OK if tail tokens are a bit higher (<=250-300ms).
4) Cost constraints: prewarmed capacity is fine but procurement needs an estimate of incremental cost vs purely autoscaled (cold starts).

I'm attaching our 72h traffic capture and a short note on session sizes. We're happy to run the PoC; procurement will want a written quote and a DocuSign for the trial terms.

Samir
Senior DevOps Engineer, AeroWorks

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: AeroWorks burst & streaming SLOs + next steps — engineering notes

Folks —

I sketched a short tech plan to validate the targets Samir called out. High level: we can meet first-token <=150ms consistently with a slightly larger warm pool + tuned batching for streaming. Details below: 

- Warm pool recommendation: start PoC with 40 prewarmed inference slices (GPU-backed; spread across 2 AZs) to keep cold-start rate <3% under 1,500 concurrent spike.
- Priming: maintain a lightweight priming KV cache per instance; run a 30-minute priming window prior to expected launch windows.
- Batching/streaming: use continuous batching with max batch size 16 and a 10ms batch window for interactive traffic; for longer replies (>200 tokens) switch to chunked streaming to reduce first-token latency impact.
- Queueing: implement priority queue with two lanes (interactive vs batch). Interactive lane size = 5k requests; batch lane soft-delay and backfill. Queue head latency target < 300 ms under burst when warm_pool_utilization > 85%.
- Scale-up tuning: autoscaler configured for aggressive ramp: detect 30% sustained increase in qps over 10s -> pre-warm an extra 20 instances; full scale-up to target within 75-90s in our tests.

Observability (metrics to collect during PoC):
- stream_first_token_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- stream_tail_token_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- cold_start_rate (per-minute)
- prewarm_utilization_pct
- queue_length & queue_latency_ms by lane
- model_variant (q4_0 vs q8) per request

I'll run a synthetic stress run on our side using the attached test harness and share prime-testing-results.csv. We should schedule a 60-minute alignment call before the PoC to lock the traffic windows and failure scenarios (AZ failure, region failover, and long-tail reply patterns).

Rishi
Senior Systems Engineer
Redwood Inference
